news.Title: Apple’s $1,999 iPhone bet just got its first answer
news.Content:
Apple (AAPL) asked consumers an unusually expensive question with the iPhone Duo: Would they pay nearly $2,000 for a phone simply because it folds?

The initial response came right away.

Preorders for Apple's first foldable iPhone opened at 8 a.m. ET on Oct. 16. Within minutes, delivery estimates moved beyond the Oct. 23 launch date, and by later that day, new online orders were backordered until late January 2027, according to CBS News . Apple described demand as "nothing short of extraordinary."

The statement does not demonstrate that Apple has made foldable phones widely available. Since launch inventory is restricted, it is hard to distinguish between low availability and true demand at this early stage.

However, that warning could be the most intriguing aspect of the narrative.

Apple priced the Duo at $1,999 for 256 gigabytes of storage, more than many laptops and substantially above a standard iPhone. The 2-terabyte version reaches $3,199. Yet customers still pushed delivery dates months into the future.

For Apple investors, the news is a first indication that the firm may have discovered something increasingly challenging in the established smartphone market: a product unique enough to persuade consumers to pay a much higher price.

Apple's iPhone Duo demand comes with an important catch

Investors should use caution when interpreting shipment delays alone, even while the presale demand seems great.

Apple has not disclosed how many iPhone Duo units were available for preorder, and supply was expected to be tighter than for a conventional iPhone launch. 9to5Mac reported that all color and storage combinations had moved to January delivery estimates within roughly 30 minutes, while noting that both demand and severe supply constraints were contributing to the delays.

That difference is important.

Selling through the first allotment would tell investors less than a comparable sale would for a regular iPhone if Apple had only prepared a comparatively limited number of Duo devices. Whether demand stays high as production catches up is what matters next.

Counterpoint Research estimated before preorders began that Apple could sell about 6 million iPhone Duo units in 2026 , depending on how quickly production ramps. That would be small compared with Apple's overall iPhone business but meaningful for a foldable category that remains niche.

Dan Ives, a partner at Yorkville Ives, is considerably more bullish. He told CBS News that he expects around 10 million Duo sales over the coming quarters and as many as 25 million in 2027.

Story Continues

That gap between six million and 25 million illustrates the question Apple still has to answer.

People will line up for the first batch, as demonstrated by the duo.

Tens of millions have not yet shown that they will purchase one.

Apple is asking buyers to pay laptop prices for an iPhone

The hardware provides Apple a rather easy pitch. The biggest display Apple has ever included on an iPhone is the 7.6-inch screen that opens from the iPhone Duo's 5.4-inch outside display. The iPhone 18 Pro Max screen is 50% smaller than the internal display, according to Apple.

More Apple:

Apple's biggest AI advantage may face new privacy challenge

Apple secret new device is a challenge to Amazon

Bank of America warns Apple investors because of Meta's Muse

The price is where the experiment becomes much more significant.

Apple starts the Duo at $1,999 for 256GB, with the 512GB version at $2,199, 1TB at $2,599 and 2TB at $3,199. MarketWatch noted that Apple is entering a category already occupied by foldable devices from Samsung and Google, but the Duo sits firmly at the expensive end of that market.

The Duo is not a must for Apple to replace the standard iPhone. The average revenue Apple receives from each premium client may be increased by a comparatively small number of consumers switching from $1,000+ regular iPhones to $1,999+ foldables.

The method is increasingly more crucial since yearly advancements in smartphones have gotten more elusive.

A new phone may be objectively improved with a quicker CPU, a somewhat better battery, or an upgraded camera without feeling all that different from the one that's currently in someone's pocket.

A phone instantly changes as it unfolds into a tablet-sized screen.

This physical distinction provides Apple what it has been looking for across the iPhone lineup: an additional incentive for consumers to upgrade.

The company is also trying to soften the headline price. Apple is offering its new Apple Upgrade leasing program starting at $57.99 per month for a 24-month Duo lease, along with trade-ins and carrier offers.

Apple has spent years educating consumers to consider phones in terms of monthly payments rather than full purchase costs. By doing the same with a foldable, an exceptionally costly gadget can seem much less unusual.

The iPhone Duo could matter even if it stays a niche product

Apple does not need every iPhone user to buy a Duo for the iPhone to be profitable.

The early demand signal is particularly intriguing because of the anticipation.

A month before preorders opened, Morningstar described the Duo as likely to remain a low-volume premium product but argued its $1,999 starting price could contribute to stronger pricing-driven iPhone growth in fiscal 2027. Morningstar raised its Apple fair-value estimate to $290 after the September launch.

Expecting the Duo to replace hundreds of millions of traditional cellphones is a distinct investment case.

Let's say Apple only sells a few million Duos. These consumers continue to spend around twice as much as the initial cost of many high-end cellphones. Additionally, Apple might provide services related to the device, storage upgrades, AppleCare, and accessories.

More significantly, the Duo creates a higher pricing point than the standard iPhone Pro.

Apple could have more space to raise its whole product mix as a result.

Another strategic benefit exists.

Foldables have been around for a long time without gaining popularity. Apple joined the market after Samsung, Google, Huawei, and other companies took on a large portion of the early engineering risk. Apple now has the opportunity to see whether its software ecosystem, existing user base, and brand can grow a market that rivals have already established.

I find it noteworthy that Apple has already passed the test's simplest form.

When the product is fresh and in limited availability, people will purchase a $1,999 foldable iPhone.

The harder test begins after Oct. 23, when the first devices reach customers and the novelty wears off.

Three factors that investors should watch are how quickly Apple clears the backlog of orders, whether production rises without declining demand, and whether customers continue to choose pricey storage options instead of just the entry model.

A presale sellout won't tell us nearly as much as those signs.

Nevertheless, Apple has gotten a positive first response to a query on which it was prepared to wager $1,999.

Customers have accepted the pricing.

Some customers are now delaying payment until 2027.

news.Title: Meta, Tesla Q3 earnings will be fighting rising AI skepticism
news.Content:
Timing is everything, and, if you're an investor in Meta Platforms ( META ) and Tesla ( TSLA ), the week ahead is a week to pay attention to their earnings reports and what company officials have to say about the state of the business.

We say that because there was a big selloff this past week in stocks related to artificial intelligence because of worries everyone involved has done what seems to be inevitable in a boom: Bet too much on a transformative technology, including data centers, and then wait for the reckoning to emerge.

The selloff came in stocks in the Nasdaq Composite Index and, in a more concentrated way, in the Nasdaq-100 stocks. The Nasdaq Composite fell 4.5% last week. The Nasdaq-100 fell 5.5%, its worst weekly loss since the Trump tariff panic in April 2025, when it fell 9.8% in a week.

The 2025 losses were soon recovered, and perhaps this past week's decline will prove a minor blip.

But it will be on everyone's minds on Oct. 21 when both Meta Platforms, the parent of Facebook and other projects, and Tesla report third quarter earnings after the close.

They are the biggest reports of the week, which will also feature reports from some of the other biggest companies including: GE Aerospace ( GE ) and Netflix ( NFLX ) on Oct. 20; Procter & Gamble ( PG ) and Blackstone ( BX ) on Oct. 22 and American Express ( AXP ) on Oct. 23.

But the Meta and Tesla reports will command intense media coverage and investor interest because of their size and market caps:

Meta's market cap is $1.8 trillion.

Tesla's market cap is $1.4 trillion, and Elon Musk's SpaceX ( SPCX ), which went public last spring, has a market cap of $1.9 trillion.

The biggest market caps belong to Nvidia ( NVDA ) and Apple ( AAPL ), both above $5 trillion.

And what investors around the world will want to know is, how exposed are Meta and Tesla to the worries that the data-center building binge will bust?

Booms and busts are a big part of capitalism. Many of us remember the dot.com boom of the late 1990s that briefly made Cisco Systems ( CSCO ) the world's most valuable company, and ultimately saw at least 1,000 companies get formed by 2000 and disappear by 2004.

The data center buildout: big and getting much bigger

Both Meta and Tesla and the rest of Elon Musk's empire are building data centers to handle artificial intelligence demands everywhere they can, while they can.

Data centers are physically huge.

And they're expensive: About $8.2 billion for a 200-megawatt AI training campus, according to a paper by Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a real estate expert at the Columbia University business school.

Story Continues

Van Nieuwerburgh estimates 188 gigawatts of new AI capacity will be completed between the end of 2025 and 2032 and another 115 GW AFTER 2032.

For the 2025-2032 period, that translates into an investment of roughly $9 trillion. That would average 3.2% of U.S. gross domestic product per year. The buildout, measured in terms of GDP, would be bigger than these U.S. economic booms:

The canal boom between 1836 and 1841: About 0.7% of estimated GDP.

The railroad boom of 1870 to 1890: About 2.2% of GDP.

The initial spread of electrification of 1905 to 1925: About 0.5% of GDP.

The highway construction boom of 1956 to 1973 (primarily, the Interstate Highway System): About 1.1% of GDP

The telecom and fiber boom of 1996 to 2003. About 1.1% of GDP.

Data centers are now so big that they've also become financially challenging.

Oracle ( ORCL ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Amazon ( AMZN ), Meta and Google-parent Alphabet ( GOOGL ) spent $97 billion on data centers in 2020 and may hit $800 billion in 2026, Van Nieuwerbergh's paper says.

The costs now are bigger than the free cash flows the companies have enjoyed for many years. And so they're bringing in investors.

Meta's Hyperion project in rural northeast Louisiana will sprawl over 3,600 acres — twice the size of Louis Armstrong International Airport in New Orleans and 25% of the size of Manhattan Island in New York.

Hyperion will be the biggest customer for New Orleans-based Entergy (ETR) . The project is expected to cost more than $50 billion, and Meta has been obliged to bring in partners to make it happen. The biggest is Blue Owl Capital ( OWL ), a New York investment management company and a giant in the private-credit industry that's been struggling to handle the stresses of aggressive growth .

Blue Owl and Meta formed a joint venture to build and operate the physical plant of the Hyperion project. Meta will own 20% of the venture (called Beignet after a donut-confection famed in New Orleans).

The venture will lease the plant to Meta over 20 years. But the lease is actually a series of four-year leases that Meta can walk away from (after making the partnership whole).

The risks to the project are big but, at least for now, manageable. But what's not known are things like:

What happens if the market for AI services slows down.

What happens if the technology driving the AI boom suddenly becomes obsolete. That affects the billions that will be invested in chips, computer servers, wiring, giant cooling systems and the like.

And, probably, what happens if the Delta country of Louisiana gets hit by massive flooding. The great 1927 flood in Louisiana affected most of the state, and the Mississippi River nearly broke out of its old channel. Had that happened, New Orleans' economy would have collapsed.

Meta's earnings won't offer much detail on these questions, but expect at least some analysts to ask CEO Mark Zuckerberg to discuss them.

The company is expected to report $6.09 a share in earnings, down 16% from a year ago, according to StockAnalysis.com . Revenue is expected to rise nearly 24% to $63.3 billion.

Meta shares are up 7.5% so far in 2026, after falling 3.7% on October 16 alone. Its performance is sixth this year among the so-called Magnificent Seven stocks.

The top performer is Apple, up 26.5%. But some other players in artificial intelligence are having great years, especially chip maker Micron, up 208% and Advance Micro Devices, up 147%.

More Artificial Intelligence:

AI's biggest business opportunity may not look like AI

AI racks are outgrowing old power: 2 chipmakers have a strategy

BofA splits software into winners and losers as AI agents arrive

Tesla faces many of the same challenges

Tesla shares have been historically volatile, and they are in 2026: down 21% on the year and down 6.4% so far in October.

The electric-vehicle maker faces some unique challenges. Its business faces intense competition globally from Chinese electric vehicle makers. And it has struggled to refresh its lineup of models for the U.S. market. That said, I see a lot of Teslas driving around Seattle.

It introduced a new generation roadster on Oct. 16, but it won't be available until 2028 at the earliest. It may include thrusters that can lift the vehicle off the ground.

The roadster reveal helped Tesla shares rise early on Oct. 16. But they fell back in the tech selloff, ending down 2.1% on the day at $354.72.

CEO Elon Musk is also polarizing, both from his work with the Trump Administration and his ability to shower favored political candidates with millions in campaign donations.

Tesla also has an additional challenge. Musk believes autonomous vehicles are the future. You call one, you get in, you get out at your destination, and the experience is supposed to be relaxing.

But how big the market really is remains unclear. I would guess it would work in large urban markets with lots of disposable income.

And Tesla is also developing a family of robots. But, like autonomous vehicles, the size of the market is not clear, and Forbes magazine notes that neither business is generating much in meaningful revenue.

news.Title: How much Amazon stock does CEO Andy Jassy actually own?
news.Content:
Andy Jassy joined Amazon in 1997 during its early years and founded the company's cloud business, which contributed significantly to its top line. Jassy eventually became CEO in 2021, and he was awarded shares in Amazon along the way as he was promoted.

Here's a closer look at how much of Amazon's stock Jassy owns, and how he accumulated his shares over the years.

How much of Amazon does Andy Jassy own?

Andy Jassy owned 2.3 million shares, directly and indirectly, according to an August 2026 SEC filing . That equates to 0.02% of the company's 10.79 billion shares outstanding. Jassy's shares were valued at about $585 million, based on a mid-October 2026 share price of $254.76.

Related: How much AMZN stock does Amazon founder Jeff Bezos actually own?

Is Andy Jassy the largest individual shareholder of Amazon?

Andy Jassy isn't the biggest shareholder of Amazon. That title belongs to Jassy's boss and Amazon founder Jeff Bezos, who owns more than 884 million shares, directly and indirectly, according to an August 2026 SEC filing . Bezos's shares equate to an 8.2% stake in the company.

How & when did Andy Jassy accumulate his Amazon stock?

Andy Jassy first joined the marketing team at Amazon in 1997, around the time the company went public. In the early 2000s, he worked closely with Bezos, and in 2006, Jassy helped establish Amazon Web Services, serving as senior vice president and becoming the division's CEO in 2016.

More on Amazon :

Who owns Amazon? Top executives and institutional investors

What is Amazon's free cash flow in 2026?

Amazon's dividends & stock splits: What you need to know

How much stock does Andy Jassy get as part of his compensation package?

As Jassy climbed the company's ranks, he was awarded shares, stock options, and restricted stock units (RSUs). In 2016, his first year as CEO of AWS, Jassy was paid a salary of $175,000, but his compensation, including stock awards, totaled $35.6 million, Amazon's 2017 proxy statement showed.

Jassy succeeded Bezos as Amazon's CEO in 2021. In 2025, his salary was $365,000, but his total compensation reached almost $2.1 million, according to Amazon's 2026 proxy statement .

At the end of 2025, Jassy's unvested stock units, or RSUs, amounted to 1.049 million shares.

Amazon's largest institutional shareholders

Institutional ownership in Amazon accounts for almost 76% of the company's 10.786 billion shares, according to data compiled by Nasdaq as of mid-October 2026. The Vanguard Group held nearly the same number of shares as Bezos, owning 845.4 million, equivalent to about a 7.8% stake.

Story Continues

The next two biggest institutional shareholders were BlackRock (6.9%) and Vanguard Capital Management (5.9%).

news.Title: Intel vs. AMD: The CPU Comeback Has Become a 2-Stock Fight, But 1 Is the Better Buy
news.Content:
The artificial intelligence (AI) boom may have first centered on GPUs, but CPUs are now in the spotlight. As AI infrastructure expands, Intel (INTC) has the chance to revive its core CPU business, while Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) is using the same demand wave to push deeper into data centers.

With the CPU comeback, both of these companies have something to prove. But one is already turning the opportunity into faster growth and stronger profits.

More News from Barchart

Why Micron Is Betting $35 Billion on Its Own Stock

Micron Stock Alert: Elon Musk Just Made The Bull Case Even Stronger

Get exclusive insights with the FREE Barchart Brief newsletter. Subscribe now for quick, incisive midday market analysis you won't find anywhere else.

The Case for Intel: AI Is Bringing Intel Back to Its Roots

When GPUs took center stage at the start of the AI boom, Intel struggled to catch up to peers like Nvidia (NVDA), AMD, Broadcom (AVGO), and Taiwan Semiconductor (TSM) which capitalized on the demand surge. But under the leadership of CEO Lip-Bu Tan, Intel is working to regain its footing and rebuild its growth story.

Intel stock has gained 144% year-to-date (YTD), suggesting investors are buying into its turnaround story.

Intel is now focusing on the business that once made it a semiconductor leader. For more than 20 years, Intel dominated the CPU market, providing chips for personal computers and enterprise servers. As AI use grows from just training models to running them and supporting more independent AI agents, the need for processing power is likely to increase. Management says demand is rising among both cloud and enterprise customers, showing that more people see how important CPUs are to AI infrastructure.

In the second quarter, Intel's Data Center and AI (DCAI) segment revenue surged 59% year-over-year (YOY) to $6.3 billion, while operating profit for the segment reached $2.5 billion. DCAI revenue also rose 24% sequentially, showing the server business is once again driving growth rather than simply serving as a legacy franchise.

Intel's manufacturing model sets it apart from AMD. It designs processors and runs its own fabrication facilities, giving it direct control over parts of production. While this is an advantage, Intel's foundry business is still operating at a loss, which stood at $2.1 billion in Q2.

Intel is therefore as much a turnaround investment as a CPU investment. Analysts predict 2026 EPS of $1.04 and 2027 EPS of $1.44, representing huge growth. Intel stock currently trades at 62.3 times forward 2027 earnings, with EPS expected to increase by 38% YOY. While the projected earnings recovery is substantial, execution risks and increasing competition remain.

Story Continues

Basically, investors are paying a premium for a recovery that hasn't materialized yet.

Overall, Wall Street remains moderately bullish about INTC stock. Of the 46 analysts covering the stock, 11 have a "Strong Buy" rating, one recommends a "Moderate Buy," 32 have a "Hold" rating, and two analysts have a "Strong Sell." The average price target of $115.58 suggests 29% potential upside from here, while the high estimate of $200 implies a 123% gain from current levels.

The Case for AMD: Already Winning More Server Business

In this CPU comeback, AMD's opportunity looks different. Although it doesn't have the legacy CPU business, it is not trying to rebuild its manufacturing operations while recovering its processor franchise. Instead, it is expanding its established EPYC server CPU business and using its broader data-center portfolio to capture more spending from cloud providers and enterprises.

AMD stock is up 147% YTD, outperforming both the broader market and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite ($NASX).

In Q2, AMD generated total revenue of $11.5 billion, up 50% YOY. Data Center revenue more than doubled to $6.7 billion, contributing roughly 58% of total revenue. The segment includes EPYC processors and Instinct AI accelerators, so its performance reflects growth across both CPU and accelerator markets. AMD has now achieved record server CPU revenue for five consecutive quarters, with cloud and enterprise sales each growing 70%-plus YOY. Management also reported gains in x86 server revenue share.

Furthermore, AMD can grow both server processors and AI accelerators. Its EPYC CPUs serve general-purpose computing needs, while its Instinct products target demanding AI workloads. The company benefits from both businesses when cloud companies expand their infrastructure.

AMD is also generating substantial profits, not just relying on revenue growth. Adjusted EPS increased 82% YOY to $1.66, while adjusted gross margin reached 56% in Q2. The company also generated $1.6 billion in free cash flow.

For fiscal 2026, analysts predict EPS of $6.49, representing 98% YOY growth. AMD stock trades at 37 times forward 2027 earnings, which are expected to rise 117% YOY. AMD is at a level of growth and profitability that Intel is still working to establish across its broader business.

Which Is the Better Buy?

Intel has a genuine comeback opportunity, but it still has a lot of things to prove. The company needs to expand output, sustain product competitiveness, and show that its manufacturing investments can generate better profits.

Meanwhile, AMD's case is pretty straightforward. Its server CPU business is gaining share, its data-center segment is growing rapidly, and its profitability shows that the expansion is already generating meaningful results. The company is even making an $8.2 billion bet on what comes next in AI by agreeing to acquire World Labs. The acquisition could help AMD anticipate how emerging technologies such as spatial intelligence, robotics, and physical AI will shape future computing needs, allowing it to align its chips and systems with the next generation of AI workloads.

Overall, AMD is my preferred pick as the stronger business to back in this CPU comeback.

Wall Street remains strongly bullish when it comes to AMD stock. Of the 47 analysts covering AMD, 37 have a "Strong Buy" rating, two recommend a "Moderate Buy," and eight recommend a "Hold." The average price target of $653.74 suggests potential upside of 24% from here, while the high price target of $1,250 suggests a possible 136% increase from current levels.

news.Title: Taiwan Semiconductor Could Partner With Elon Musk’s Terafab, but It Has 1 Condition
news.Content:
Elon Musk wants to build his own chip factory, and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TSM) could be a key partner. But Taiwan's largest company has drawn a line it will not cross.

The two sides are reportedly discussing Terafab, Musk's Texas chip project. What we do know is they disagree on one key element: who runs the factory?

More News from Barchart

Intel vs. AMD: The CPU Comeback Has Become a 2-Stock Fight, But 1 Is the Better Buy

Micron Stock Alert: Elon Musk Just Made The Bull Case Even Stronger

Dear Sandisk Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendar for October 29

Get exclusive insights with the FREE Barchart Brief newsletter. Subscribe now for quick, incisive midday market analysis you won't find anywhere else.

TSMC and Terafab Are Talking, but Who Runs the Fab?

Bloomberg reported that TSMC is in talks about working with Terafab. The project is Musk's effort to manufacture chips for Tesla (TSLA), SpaceX (SPCX), and xAI. Intel (INTC) will help develop the Terafab plant technology.

Notably, TSMC CEO C.C. Wei confirmed the talks on TSMC's third-quarter earnings call on Oct. 15. Then he added the condition, stating:

"But the fab has got to be run by TSMC."

Last week, Musk said TSMC would lease capacity at most and stressed that his companies would "build and run the fab," Bloomberg reported. An analyst asked whether it would look like TSMC's ventures in Japan and Europe. Wei said it could go either way, but TSMC must be the operator.

Why TSMC Will Not Hand Over the Keys

TSMC explained that the key reason is efficiency. CFO Wendell Huang said TSMC remains the most cost-efficient manufacturer in every region it operates. Huang said overseas fabs will cut gross margin by close to 2% in 2026. As more U.S. fabs ramp up production, he expects that drag to widen to 3% to 4% in the next few years.

So TSMC is already paying a premium to build in America, and letting someone else run a plant would put its core strength in an outsider's hands.

TSMC can afford to be picky.

Here is what the third quarter looked like, given its continued steady growth.

Here's how it performed in Q3 of 2026:

Revenue: $46.7 billion, up 16.2% from Q2 and above guidance.

Gross margin: 66.4%, down 1.3 points because of the 2-nanometer ramp.

Operating margin: 58.7%. So, TSMC kept about 59 cents of every revenue dollar as operating profit.

Earnings per share: $0.91 (TWD 29.43).

Cash from operations: about $28.5 billion (TWD 920 billion).

High-performance computing, the chip category that includes AI, accounted for 68% of revenue. TSMC guided fourth-quarter revenue to between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion. At the midpoint, that is a 58% jump from the year-ago period. Wei now expects full-year 2026 revenue growth of around 44%.

Story Continues

TSMC also reiterated a 2026 capital budget of $60 billion to $64 billion. In Q3, it spent nearly $14 billion on capital expenditures.

Texas Fits Expansion Plans

Wei said most of TSMC's large customers are in the U.S., and they have asked for more "American" capacity. TSMC has now looked beyond Arizona. Wei said the company sent teams to Texas to evaluate sites. He also said TSMC spoke with a customer building a fab, and Wei named Terafab as a potential opportunity.

TSMC finished building its second Arizona fab, and volume production of 3-nanometer chips is set for the third quarter of 2027, slightly ahead of schedule. Worldwide, nearly 20 fabs are under construction because of strong demand from multiple AI companies.

Is TSM Stock Still a Good Buy?

A deal with Terafab would increase U.S.-origin demand at a time when customers want domestic capacity. However, margin pressure from overseas fabs is set to grow. Wei also warned that consumer and price-sensitive markets are under strain.

TSMC is being prudent in its prospects because of higher prices, making control of the plant even more important.

Analysts expect AI-fueled growth for TSMC to continue through 2030. Wall Street expects revenue to grow from $120.6 billion in 2025 to $413 billion in 2030. Over this period, net income is projected to expand from $54.4 billion to $197 billion. If TSM stock is priced at 18x forward earnings, similar to its five-year average, it could surge 75% from current levels.

Out of the 19 analysts covering TSM stock, 16 recommend "Strong Buy," two recommend "Moderate Buy," and one recommends "Hold." The average TSM price target is $523, above the current price of about $414.

news.Title: AI Sector Pressure, Earnings and Other Key Things to Watch this Week
news.Content:
Markets enter a heavy earnings week with Meta Platforms (META), Tesla (TSLA), Netflix (NFLX) and Texas Instruments (TXN) reporting alongside Wednesday's crude oil inventories. Semiconductor pressure and AI spending doubts remain front and center. Crude volatility and geopolitical risk continue to shape the inflation backdrop. Rising bond yields are keeping Fed expectations in focus. Friday's flash PMI readings close out a week that could set the tone into late October.

Here are 5 things to watch this week in the Market.

More News from Barchart

Intel vs. AMD: The CPU Comeback Has Become a 2-Stock Fight, But 1 Is the Better Buy

Micron Stock Alert: Elon Musk Just Made The Bull Case Even Stronger

Dear Sandisk Stock Fans, Mark Your Calendar for October 29

Tired of missing midday reversals? The FREE Barchart Brief newsletter keeps you in the know. Sign up now!

AI and Semiconductor Sector Pressure

Meta (META) reports Wednesday, and investors will focus on AI capital spending. The question is whether spending is translating into revenue growth. Texas Instruments (TXN) also reports Wednesday. Its results offer a read on analog chip demand. Lam Research (LRCX) reports the same day, giving insight into chip equipment orders. Strong results could steady the sector. Weak guidance would deepen concerns about AI returns. Semiconductor stocks have been volatile, and earnings will set the tone.

Crude Oil Volatility and Geopolitical Risk

Wednesday's crude oil inventories at 10:30am will show supply and demand trends. Oil prices remain sensitive to Middle East developments. Escalation risks could push prices higher quickly. Higher energy costs would feed inflation and complicate the Fed's path. Valero (VLO) reports Thursday, offering a read on refining margins. Strong margins would signal healthy fuel demand. Exxon-linked energy names have been sensitive to every headline, so position sizing matters.

Rising Bond Yields and Fed Expectations

Bond yields continue to influence equity valuations. Higher yields compress multiples, especially for growth stocks. Investors are watching whether the Fed will hold or lean hawkish. Thursday's jobless claims at 8:30am offer a weekly read on labor conditions. Stronger labor data would support the case for higher-for-longer rates. Weaker claims could ease pressure on yields. Bank earnings from earlier in the month have already shown mixed loan demand. Yield direction will likely drive sector rotation this week.

Consumer and Industrial Earnings Read-Through

Story Continues

Netflix (NFLX) and General Motors (GM) report Tuesday. Netflix will show whether streaming demand holds up. GM will show auto demand and pricing. Procter & Gamble (PG) reports Thursday and offers a read on household spending. Lockheed Martin (LMT) and RTX (RTX) bring defence and geopolitical sensitivity into focus. Mixed consumer results would reinforce the stagflation debate.

Friday Flash PMI Readings

Friday's preliminary October Manufacturing and Services PMI readings at 9:45am will give the first look at October activity. Manufacturing data will show whether factories are expanding or contracting. Services data covers the largest part of the economy. Strong readings would ease recession worries. Weak readings would raise questions about the Fed's next move. Investors will weigh these numbers against the week's earnings and oil headlines before the next set of reports.

Best of luck this week and don't forget to check out my daily options article.

news.Title: Broadcom (AVGO) Went Nowhere for a Year. Analysts Think It Is Worth 50% More
news.Content: Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ: AVGO ) closed at $344.33 on October 15. The stock has returned -13.59% over the last six months, compared to a 15.4% return for the Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and 11.4% for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust. Broadcom sells two things mainly that have little to do with each other. It designs chips, including the custom processors that large technology companies order instead of buying standard parts. It also sells infrastructure software to corporate customers, a business it assembled through acquisitions. The chips are the larger half and the reason anyone follows the stock. What makes the past year strange is that the business grew at a pace few companies this size manage, and the share price finished where it started. As per CNN, analysts covering the stock put their median target 52.47% above where it trades now. READ ALSO: 12 Most Profitable American Stocks to Buy in 2026 The Business Did Not Go Nowhere: Revenue in the most recent quarter was 85.5% higher than a year earlier. Earnings grew 216.1% over the same stretch. Those are not the numbers of a company treading water. The custom chip business explains most of it. When a large technology firm decides it wants its own processor rather than a standard one, it comes to a small number of designers, and Broadcom is the largest of them. That work is also sticky in a way ordinary chip sales are not. A customer that commits to a custom design cannot change supplier without starting the engineering again. Broadcom appears alongside the other names analysts see the most room in through our 10 Most Promising Technology Stocks to Buy Right Now . To see which ones, click HERE . Why the Shares Did Not Follow: The stock has fallen 1.43% over twelve months while the business behind it roughly doubled, and all of that decline has come in the past six months. One explanation is that the price had already moved before the growth arrived, and the past year has been the company catching up to its own valuation rather than the other way round. The multiple supports that reading. Broadcom trades at 46.50 times what it earned over the past year, which is a demanding figure even after a flat twelve months. There is a concentration problem too. The custom chip customers are a handful of very large companies with the resources to bring the work in-house if they ever decide to. Growth of this kind depends on a few decisions made in a few places. DON'T MISS: 10 AI Stocks Beyond Nvidia That Could Surge in 2026 Story Continues The Gap Between the Two Multiples: The forward multiple tells a different story from the trailing one. The shares sit at 19.42 times what analysts expect next year, less than half the trailing figure. The market expects earnings to keep climbing steeply. The two numbers cannot both be right for long. Either the earnings arrive, and the trailing multiple falls towards the forward one, or they do not and the forward figure drifts back up. A year that went nowhere has quietly turned an expensive stock into a cheaper-looking one without settling which it is. Check Our: 10 Best Mortgage Finance Stocks To Buy According to Billionaires Conclusion: A year of nothing is an unusual thing to happen to a company growing this fast. It means the share price ended the year where it started while the earnings underneath it climbed, which is the arithmetic that makes a stock cheaper without anyone selling it. The question is whether the custom chip orders keep coming from the same small group of buyers. If they do, the gap that has opened is an opportunity. If they slow, the trailing multiple is the one that matters. Market Sentiment: Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) was held by 170 hedge funds with a combined stake value of about $29.08 billion at the end of Q2 2026 in the Insider Monkey database. This is down from 173 hedge fund holders with a cumulative investment value of around $32.84 billion in the previous quarter. While we acknowledge the potential of AVGO as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. news.Title: What Is Applied Materials’ (AMAT) Economic Moat, and Is It Widening or Narrowing?
news.Content:
Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMAT ) closed at $430.01 on October 15. The stock returned 9.1% over the last 6 months, compared with a 15.4% return for the Insider Monkey Billionaire Index and 11.4% for the State Street SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust.

Applied Materials does not make chips. It makes the machines that make them. A modern chip plant runs hundreds of separate steps, and Applied supplies equipment across more of them than its big rivals do, each of which tends to specialize in one or two. That breadth is most of the argument for the company. Whether it amounts to a moat depends on how hard it would be for a customer to buy those machines somewhere else.

READ ALSO: 10 Best Stocks to Buy for High Returns in 2026

Why the Position Is Hard to Attack:

Switching equipment is not like switching suppliers. A chipmaker qualifies a machine over months, tunes a recipe around it, and then builds a production line that depends on it behaving identically every time. Changing it means proving the whole process again.

Breadth compounds that. A customer buying across many steps from one supplier gets machines designed to work together, and the firm selling them learns things about the customer's process that a single-step rival never sees.

The financial evidence is consistent with a strong position. Operating margin runs at 33.74% and return on equity at 41.07%, which is unusual for a business selling heavy industrial equipment. Applied Materials appears in our 10 Most Promising Technology Stocks to Buy Right Now , where analysts see a wider gap in five other names. To see them, click HERE .

Where the Moat Is Narrowing:

The advantage does not extend to every step. The most advanced patterning machines come from a single Dutch company that Applied does not compete with, and that step has become the one that defines what a leading chip plant can do.

Customer concentration is the second pressure. A small number of chipmakers account for most of the spending on advanced equipment, and each of them is large enough to push hard on price.

Then there is politics. Equipment sales are governed by export rules, and which customers a firm may sell to is decided by governments rather than by the firm. That is a risk no amount of engineering advantage offsets.

DON'T MISS: 10 Most Profitable Undervalued Stocks to Invest In

What the Shares Are Asking:

Applied trades at 23.42 times what analysts expect next year. The stock is up 88.83% over twelve months and still sits well below its high, so the market has already had both opinions about it within the same year.

Story Continues

Set that against 36.01 times the past year and a sizeable step up in earnings is already assumed. That step depends on how much a handful of customers choose to spend, which is a decision nobody at Applied makes.

Check out: 10 Best Mortgage Finance Stocks To Buy According to Billionaires

Conclusion:

The moat is real, and it is built on the difficulty of changing a qualified machine, not on anything proprietary about the physics. On the evidence, it is holding rather than widening, because the step that now matters most belongs to someone else and the customer base is concentrating rather than spreading. The thing to watch is capital spending plans at the big chipmakers, since that is the number this business converts into revenue.

Market Sentiment:

Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ:AMAT) was held by 137 hedge funds with a combined stake value of about $16.71 billion at the end of Q2 2026 in the Insider Monkey database. This is down from 138 hedge fund holders with a cumulative investment value of around $10.33 billion in the previous quarter.

While we acknowledge the potential of AMAT as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. news.Title: Chip toolmakers can’t catch a break, even as TSMC spends more
news.Content: In January, one spending forecast from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. (TSM) helped make ASML, the world's largest chip equipment maker, become a $500 billion company. When TSMC planned to spend $52 billion to $56 billion earlier in 2026, above the $46 billion analysts expected, according to Reuters , ASML Holding N.V. (ASML), whose top customer is TSMC, crossed the $500 billion mark for the first time that day. Nine months later, TSMC made a bigger version of the same promise. This time, its suppliers' stocks went the other way. On Thursday, October 15, 2026, TSMC reiterated a 2026 budget of $60 billion to $64 billion on its earnings call . Chief Financial Officer Wendell Huang said spending from 2026 through 2028 should run significantly higher than the prior three years. The toolmakers fell harder than TSMC did. TSMC's Taiwan-listed shares slipped 2% on Thursday, according to Morningstar . Applied Materials Inc. (AMAT) closed 3.7% lower, extending an eight-session losing streak. Lam Research Corp. (LRCX) closed lower for a ninth straight session . That had never happened since its 1984 listing, according to Benzinga . When a bigger promise produces a deeper selloff, the market has stopped pricing the promise itself. Also read: TSMC's $46.7 billion quarter leaves 1 question for investors TSMC is the world's largest contract chipmaker, and Chief Executive C.C. Wei said all the AI players work with it. That reach makes its capital budget the closest thing chip toolmakers have to a public order book. The quarter itself gave investors little to fear Third-quarter revenue reached $46.72 billion, up 41% from a year earlier, according to TSMC's press release . Huang said that it topped the company's own forecast range, a sign that demand outran even TSMC's planning. The outlook was stronger still. TSMC guided fourth-quarter revenue of $52.3 billion to $54.3 billion, above the $50.5 billion analysts expected, according to Seeking Alpha . That tells suppliers the order flow is not peaking this quarter. The soft spot was margin. Gross margin slipped to 66.4% from 67.7% in the second quarter, Seeking Alpha reported . Huang tied the dip to the early ramp of TSMC's 2-nanometer process, which points to expansion costs rather than weak pricing. Equipment stocks were falling before TSMC reported Applied Materials fell nearly 7% on Tuesday, October 13, 2026, after declining to forecast industry tool spending, according to Benzinga . That cost investors a key benchmark for sizing the equipment market. Story Continues The next day, ASML posted record quarterly sales. Its results filing said planned supply for 2027 and 2028 "will not fully meet the demand of our customers." A supplier sold out two years ahead is about as bullish as equipment news gets. More TSMC: TSMC's $46.7 billion quarter leaves 1 question for investors TSMC's rivals are losing ground, and the gap is growing Chip stocks set for $229 billion payday before Nvidia ships a GPU The selling continued anyway. A hotter U.S. inflation reading added to rate-hike bets and Fed worries about AI debt, Morningstar reported . A Wednesday social media post about the debt load of AI cloud provider CoreWeave Inc. (CRWV) sharpened those worries. Selling soon spread to hardware suppliers, SiliconANGLE reported . Toolmakers sit at the far end of that financing chain. Cloud builders borrow, chip designers order wafers, and only then does TSMC buy machines. When money gets pricier, investors tend to sell the end of the chain first. TSMC is watching that chain closely. Wei said it now sends its own teams to check U.S. data center construction and power supply, with good feedback so far. TSMC is squeezing more out of tools it already owns Wei said TSMC keeps converting 5-nanometer tools to 3-nanometer work and shifting capacity among its 7-, 5-, and 3-nanometer lines. Every reused tool is one TSMC does not need to buy new. Huang also said revenue growth should outpace capital spending growth if TSMC executes well. That means TSMC's budget can keep climbing while claiming a smaller slice of its sales. Three other signals stood out: Tool prices are climbing. Huang said tool supply is tight and that "tool price inflation is real." Overseas factories will cost more. Huang said margin dilution from fabs outside Taiwan should widen by 3 to 4 percentage points in the next few years. Leading-edge capacity keeps growing. Wei said annual capacity for TSMC's 2-nanometer family should more than double in 2027. Higher tool prices can still boost supplier revenue even as TSMC stretches older equipment. Yet growth driven more by price than by volume leaves less of a cushion if orders slow. Equipment stocks now need orders, not promises Lam Research reports September-quarter results on Wednesday, October 21, 2026, after guiding for $8.1 billion in revenue, Benzinga reported . UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri expects the season to turn on capacity plans and margins, not quarterly numbers, the outlet added. Even after Thursday's drop, Lam was still up 60% this year, Benzinga noted. That echoes the question over TSMC's own record quarter: whether the good news was already priced in . January treated a capital budget as income for suppliers. October treated it as a cost that someone still has to finance. Markets can stop rewarding spending plans long before companies stop making them. Equipment makers sit furthest from the end customer, so they often feel that shift first. TSMC has promised to keep spending through 2028, and its suppliers now have to prove that promise one order at a time. news.Title: Own VGT? Here's How Much of It Is Really Nvidia, Apple, Microsoft, and Broadcom.
news.Content: When investing in tech exchange-traded funds (ETFs), sometimes it's a good idea to peek under the hood and see what you're really buying within each fund's portfolio. Sometimes there is a lot of overlap from one tech ETF to another. This can make it easier to choose the best tech ETF for your goals, based on which fund holds which mix of stocks and sectors. The Vanguard Information Technology ETF (NYSEMKT: VGT) is a popular tech fund that holds 318 stocks. It represents a wide range of companies in the electronics and computer industries, including semiconductors , software, hardware, and tech-related services and components. And VGT is a passive index fund, so it doesn't pick stocks -- it just tracks the performance of its tech sector benchmark. Missed Nvidia in 2009? This Rare Signal Is Flashing Again. In 2009, a "Double Down" signal flashed for a little-known chipmaker called Nvidia. For the first time in years, that same "Total Conviction" signal is flashing for a company 1/100th the size of Nvidia. Continue » When you buy VGT, you're going to get a strong concentration of major tech names that are also top holdings in the S&P 500 index (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) and Nasdaq-100 index. But how much of VGT is just a few major tech stocks that you can buy in other ETFs? A large percentage of assets of the Vanguard Information Technology ETF is made up of only four big-name tech tickers: Nvidia (NASDAQ: NVDA), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), and Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO). As of Sept. 30, those four stocks represented about 49% of the VGT fund's assets. If you feel like VGT is getting too top-heavy with just these four tech names, or you want to own a different mix of stocks, this could affect your investment choices. Let's take a closer look at VGT and its concentration of tech majors NVDA, AAPL, MSFT, and AVGO. Vanguard Information Technology ETF (VGT): 22 years of 15% annualized returns The Vanguard Information Technology ETF has delivered strong returns for investors, with average annual returns of 15.03% since the fund's inception in January 2004. It's done even better in the past few years, with about 24.7% annualized returns in the past 10 years, 20.9% in the past five years, 35% in the past three years, and about 35.2% in the past year. Unlike many popular tech ETFs, VGT is somewhat unique for some of the well-known "Magnificent Seven" tech stocks that it does not own. For example, the VGT fund does not hold Alphabet , Amazon , Meta Platforms , or Tesla . That's because although these companies are frequently described as "tech stocks," they are not technically part of the information technology sector as defined by the MSCI US IMI Information Technology 25/50 Index , which is the benchmark that VGT follows. Story Continues But the mix of growth stocks in VGT has been pretty successful. VGT has strongly outperformed the Nasdaq-100 during the past 10 years. The Vanguard Information Technology ETF is no exception to that trend. But if you're concerned about making too concentrated an investment in just four stocks, this could be worth paying attention to. news.Title: $3,000 Split Across Nvidia, Broadcom, and TSMC Could Be Worth This Much by 2030

With that amount, you could buy five shares of Nvidia, three of Broadcom, and two of TSMC for under $3,000.

If the AI infrastructure build-out continues, I think that investment could be worth over $9,000 by the end of 2030, a more-than-threefold return in a little over four years. news.Title: Jim Cramer Sees a Telling Change in Broadcom’s (AVGO) Stock
news.Content: During the October 6 episode of Mad Money, a caller expressed frustration that Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ: AVGO ) had "hardly moved." Jim Cramer responded: Okay, Jeff Marks and I, you know, runs the Trust with me, we talk about it every day. I said, "Can you believe it? Broadcom is up." And he said, "Yeah, it's finally going up. It's above where it was when it reported." Now, what happens when you see that?... When you see that it's now above where it was when it reported the so-called bad quarter, it means the prospects are probably better. Don't sell it here. I did trim because we have so much of these, but I'm not going to sell the rest. I'd say ride it with me. Cramer had already challenged the market's reaction to Broadcom's earnings in September. His earlier assessment of the selloff explained why he thought investors were placing too much weight on one part of its outlook. Broadcom also earned a place in our list of 10 Best AI Infrastructure Stocks to Buy for the Long Term. See which other stocks made the list. Custom AI Chips Continue to Drive Growth Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) reported fiscal third-quarter 2026 revenue of approximately $29.6 billion, up 86% year over year. AI semiconductor revenue increased 221% to $16.7 billion, with management pointing to demand for custom accelerators and networking products. Infrastructure software revenue also grew 29% to approximately $8.75 billion. Custom chips and networking give Broadcom two routes into AI infrastructure spending. Its inclusion in a broader selection of AI stocks places it along with companies pursuing other parts of that opportunity. The company generated approximately $13.7 billion in free cash flow, equivalent to 46% of revenue. Adjusted earnings reached $3.32 per share, compared with GAAP earnings of $2.68. For the fourth quarter, management projected approximately $34.8 billion in total revenue, including $21.7 billion from AI semiconductors. These are substantial growth figures despite the disappointing stock reaction described by Cramer. The Valuation Still Depends on Delivering Growth Broadcom trades at approximately 21.7x forward earnings, compared with 19.6x for the semiconductor kingpin, NVIDIA. Broadcom also traded at approximately 11.5x forward sales versus NVIDIA's 10.7x. NVIDIA provides a relevant AI semiconductor comparison, although Broadcom's infrastructure software business makes their revenue and profit mixes different. Broadcom does not offer a clear valuation discount to this major AI peer. NVIDIA is one useful benchmark, but the AI investment universe extends well beyond the two chipmakers. Story Continues Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ:AVGO) identifies fluctuations in major customers' orders and dependence on a limited number of suppliers as business risks. Its reliance on outsourced manufacturing also makes production capacity and accurate demand forecasts important. Margin expectations deserve attention as well. Fourth-quarter adjusted operating margin guidance of approximately 66% is below the roughly 67.9% calculated from third-quarter adjusted operating income and revenue. It is important to know that higher sales do not necessarily mean a higher margin in every quarter. Hedge Fund Participation Remains Broad According to Insider Monkey, 170 hedge funds held Broadcom in Q2, down from 173 in Q1. With 15.13 million shares, Fisher Asset Management took the top spot among the 1000+ hedge funds tracked by Insider Monkey. Short interest stood at 1.11% of the float, highlighting limited short positioning relative to available shares. Cramer has reduced his position, but he remains willing to hold the rest. Broadcom's AI revenue and cash generation might be able to explain that confidence. With the stock still valued above NVIDIA on these forward measures, the next earnings reports will need to sustain the growth expectations behind it. While we acknowledge the potential of AVGO as an investment, we believe certain AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. news.Title: Lam Research vs. Applied Materials: Which Buybacks Are Better Covered by Cash?
news.Content:
Lam Research and Applied Materials belong to our 10 Best AI Infrastructure Stocks to Buy for the Long Term . Both return cash while investing in semiconductor equipment, but the latest cash statements give Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMAT ) more room after shareholder payouts than Lam Research Corporation (NASDAQ: LRCX ). The comparison changes when a single quarter is widened to a full year.

Photo from AAOI

Compare payouts after investment

Lam generated $1.457 billion of operating cash in its quarter ended June 28. Subtracting $188.8 million spent on capital expenditure and intangible assets leaves $1.268 billion. Treasury-stock purchases, including excise tax, were $246.6 million, and dividends were $325.3 million. Together, those payments consumed 45.1% of the residual cash.

Applied generated $3.037 billion of operating cash in its quarter ended July 26. After $707 million of capital expenditure, $2.330 billion remained. Repurchases of $440 million and dividends of $420 million consumed 36.9%. Applied therefore retained a larger share of cash after investment and payouts in these latest, differently dated quarters.

That is coverage of actual payments. Buyback authorizations do not require immediate spending. Both companies can adjust repurchases when equipment demand or investment needs change; dividends and buybacks should not be treated as identical commitments.

Lam's full-year record changes the picture

For its fiscal year ended June 28, Lam generated $5.858 billion of operating cash and spent $966.4 million on capital expenditure and intangibles, leaving $4.891 billion. Repurchases and dividends totaled $5.122 billion, exceeding that residual by about $231 million. Its restrained final quarter therefore did not mean the full year's payouts were entirely covered by that year's cash after investment.

This does not establish financial distress: accumulated cash can fund distributions, and working-capital timing affects annual cash generation. It does mean investors should test payout coverage across periods.

On October 16, the trailing free-cash-flow multiples were at 69 for Lam and 59 for Applied. A better-covered payout does not automatically make either stock cheap. Our equipment analysis asks when faster growth fails to justify a higher cash-flow price . Investment timing and working capital can move those historical multiples sharply.

Q2 2026 hedge-fund holders rose to 139 from 123 for Lam and slipped to 137 from 138 for Applied. Arrowstreet reduced Lam shares 7%; Coatue reduced Applied shares 20%. The tracked fund population changed between quarters. September 30 short interest was 2.1% and 1.7% of float, respectively.

Story Continues

Applied has the stronger latest-quarter payout coverage on this measure. Lam's full-year excess makes sustained collections and disciplined repurchases more important. Lam could improve coverage through stronger cash conversion or lower payouts; Applied could lose its advantage if investment rises faster than collections. Investors should watch cash after investment across several quarters, alongside the price paid for that cash.

While we acknowledge the potential of LRCX and AMAT as investments, we believe certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. news.Title: Lam Research vs. Applied Materials: How Much Protection Does the Installed Base Offer?
news.Content:
Both Lam Research Corporation (NASDAQ: LRCX ) and Applied Materials, Inc. (NASDAQ: AMAT ) serve customers building more complex chips, but investors also need to know what survives a pause in new equipment orders. The companies rank seventh and eighth, respectively, in our 10 Best AI Infrastructure Stocks to Buy for the Long Term , which identifies six higher-ranked infrastructure businesses. An accounting distinction between the two adds another layer to the comparison.

Wichy/Shutterstock.com

The service labels cover different businesses

Lam reported $6.722 billion of revenue for its June quarter on July 29. Customer support and other revenue contributed $2.472 billion, or 36.8%; systems supplied the balance. That support category includes mature-node Reliant equipment alongside service-related activity, so treating all of it as recurring maintenance overstates the cushion.

Applied's August 13 release showed $9.115 billion of July-quarter revenue. Applied Global Services supplied $1.781 billion, or 19.5%, and $536 million of operating profit. Its operating margin was 30.1%, versus 27.3% a year earlier. Applied moved its 200mm equipment business into Semiconductor Systems starting in fiscal 2026 and recast the comparison periods.

The percentages therefore cannot establish that Lam has nearly twice Applied's recurring-service protection. Both installed bases create demand for support and upgrades; customer utilization and the equipment included in each segment still matter.

A revenue cushion is not an earnings floor

If Lam's systems revenue fell 10% while support and other revenue stayed flat, total sales would fall 6.3%. If Applied's Semiconductor Systems sales fell 10% while all other revenue stayed flat, its total would fall 7.7%. These are mechanical scenarios using the reported segment mix, not predictions. Service and mature-node equipment demand can also decline, and fixed expenses can make profit fall faster than revenue.

Lam's reported GAAP operating margin was 37.4%, against Applied's 33.7%. Advanced chip complexity supports both businesses, but spending delays, export restrictions and customer concentration can impair that opportunity. Our Lam-KLA comparison examines when faster equipment growth stops justifying a higher cash-flow price .

October 15 trailing cash-flow multiples were about 71 for Lam and 61 for Applied. Such valuations require durable cash generation; the segment exercise alone cannot identify the better-priced stock. Different working-capital cycles and investment timing also affect those multiples.

Story Continues

Q2 2026 hedge-fund holders increased to 139 from 123 for Lam, while Applied slipped to 137 from 138. Arrowstreet reduced Lam shares 7%; Coatue cut Applied shares 20%. September 30 short interest represented 2.07% and 1.7% of float, respectively.

Lam's reported mix provides a larger mechanical buffer against a systems-only decline. Applied offers a cleaner view of its reshaped services business. Investors should favor evidence that service profit and cash persist through weaker equipment orders; a larger category labeled support is insufficient by itself.

news.Title: Broadcom’s $29 Billion AI Backstop: How Much Risk Does the Cash Flow Cover?
news.Content:
Broadcom Inc. (NASDAQ: AVGO ) generates substantial cash, but how should investors size the risk it takes when a customer's compute leases need backing? The company ranks sixth in our 10 Best AI Infrastructure Stocks to Buy for the Long Term, despite having more hedge-fund holders than all but three companies on the list. The key concern for AVGO is how much financial exposure it faces if the customer struggles to meet its lease obligations.

Photo by Sergei Starostin on Pexels

The maximum is not the expected bill

Broadcom's quarterly filing for the period ended August 2 describes a backstop covering a customer's five-year lease obligations. Exposure rises as racks are deployed and falls as lease payments arrive. In a default, the liability reflects 85% of outstanding covered amounts less proceeds from the equipment. The maximum potential liability after full deployment was about $29 billion, undiscounted; no payments had been made, and the recorded fair value was immaterial.

The filing also describes conditional financing through customer convertible notes of up to $42 billion, with none issued at August 2. This related commitment is not automatically additive debt or an incurred loss.

Those distinctions matter. Treating $29 billion as ordinary debt overstates a contingent obligation; ignoring it because the initial accounting value is small overlooks a potentially significant downside claim. Equipment resale, lease assumption and contractual remedies can reduce losses. Their effectiveness depends on the assets and market conditions when a default occurs.

Cash generation provides scale, not immunity

Broadcom generated $13.665 billion of free cash flow in its latest quarter. The maximum backstop equals 2.12 such quarters, or 53% of four times that quarterly cash figure. Annualizing one quarter is only a scale comparison: a credit shock could also weaken chip demand and cash generation. Cash was $23.975 billion at August 2, below the maximum backstop. That cash also supports debt and ordinary business obligations.

AI semiconductor revenue reached $16.7 billion in the quarter, supporting the case that custom accelerators and networking can finance continued growth. Customer concentration creates the opposing risk. Our Nvidia comparison examines how financing exposure changes the choice between two leading AI chip suppliers .

At October 15 prices, Broadcom traded around 42 times trailing free cash flow. That valuation leaves investors reliant on continued growth, while the contingent exposure can worsen an adverse demand scenario. Q2 2026 hedge-fund holders fell to 170 from 173, although Fisher increased shares 3%. September 30 short interest was 1.16% of float.

Story Continues

Whether the backstop is manageable depends on recoveries, deployment and cash generation when stress arrives. The useful next evidence is the amount actually deployed, customer payments and any change in guarantee exposure. Current cash flow supplies meaningful capacity, but it cannot make the maximum obligation harmless.

While we acknowledge the potential of AVGO as an investment, we believe certain other AI stocks offer greater upside potential and carry less downside risk. news.Title: Why Broadcom Stock Is a Good Buy Now
news.Content:
Broadcom (AVGO) stock has fallen more than 30% from its high on concerns about the sustainability of artificial intelligence (AI) spending and intensifying competition in the custom AI chip market. While AVGO stock has pulled back, the company's growth prospects remain solid.

Broadcom continues to benefit from strong demand for AI infrastructure, expanding relationships with major technology companies, and growing adoption of its custom accelerators and networking solutions. Further, the decline in its share price has made Broadcom's valuation more attractive.

More News from Barchart

Cathie Wood Is Avoiding Micron. Micron Bulls Might Want to Celebrate

Why Micron Is Betting $35 Billion on Its Own Stock

Micron Stock Alert: Elon Musk Just Made The Bull Case Even Stronger

Stop Missing Market Moves: Get the FREE Barchart Brief – your midday dose of stock movers, trending sectors, and actionable trade ideas, delivered right to your inbox. Sign Up Now!

XPUs to Power Broadcom Higher

Broadcom's custom AI accelerators, known as XPUs, are emerging as a major driver of its growth.

The company's latest reported quarterly results and outlook reflect the scale of this opportunity. AI semiconductor revenue rose 221% year-over-year (YoY) and 54% sequentially to $16.7 billion.

Custom accelerators are playing a key role in its growth. Shipments to Broadcom's six XPU customers rose more than 3.5 times YoY and accounted for about 73% of its AI revenue during the quarter. AI networking revenue also grew more than 2.5 times over the same period, reflecting strong demand for the infrastructure needed to support AI workloads.

The planned product deployments across several major AI and cloud computing companies strengthen Broadcom's growth outlook. The company expects to increase shipments of Ironwood accelerators to Anthropic, expand high-volume deliveries of its eighth-generation TPU products to Alphabet's (GOOG) (GOOGL) Google, continue shipments of custom chips for OpenAI, and begin production shipments of Meta's (META) MTIA accelerators for inference and recommendation workloads.

These deployments highlight the breadth of Broadcom's custom AI opportunity and ease competition concerns.

Broadcom's product pipeline and expanding deployments suggest that demand remains strong. Management expects both XPU and AI networking revenue to triple YoY in the fourth quarter. Based on this, the company projects quarterly AI revenue of $21.7 billion, representing annual growth of 236%.

Broadcom's expanding product pipeline and growing customer deployments suggest that demand for its AI solutions remains strong. Management expects both XPU and AI networking revenue to triple YoY in the fourth quarter. As a result, the company projects quarterly AI revenue of $21.7 billion, representing 236% annual growth.

Story Continues

The longer-term outlook points to an even larger opportunity. Management expects AI revenue to reach $58 billion in fiscal 2026, up 186% YoY and above its previous forecast of $56 billion.

Looking further ahead, Broadcom expects AI revenue to double to $115 billion in fiscal 2027 and then double again to $230 billion in fiscal 2028. Continued demand for custom AI accelerators and growing sales of AI networking products are expected to drive this expansion.

Strong AI semiconductor revenue and operating leverage are also expected to support significant earnings growth. Management anticipates that earnings per share (EPS) will exceed $30 in fiscal 2028, marking a substantial increase from current levels.

For context, analysts expect Broadcom to report EPS of $17.45 in fiscal 2027. If Broadcom achieves EPS of $30 in fiscal 2028, that would represent approximately 72% YoY growth. This would be notable given the increasingly challenging comparisons Broadcom faces as its earnings base expands. Analysts already expect EPS to grow by more than 84% in fiscal 2026 and 68% in fiscal 2027.

Overall, solid demand for Broadcom's custom AI accelerators and AI networking solutions, expanding customer relationships, and operating leverage position the company for substantial revenue and earnings growth over the next several years.

Broadcom's Valuation Offers Potential Upside

Broadcom is well-positioned to deliver strong earnings growth in the coming years. At the same time, its current valuation appears low and attractive relative to its growth prospects. AVGO shares trade at 34.2 times forward earnings, a relatively modest multiple given the company's strong earnings growth outlook.

Moreover, Broadcom trades at a significant discount to peers such as Marvell (MRVL), which commands a forward price-to-earnings multiple of 87.2. This valuation gap and solid earnings growth trajectory suggest that Broadcom has upside potential.

Buy AVGO Stock Now

Broadcom's strong AI revenue growth, expanding XPU deployments, and rising demand for AI networking solutions provide a solid foundation for sustained earnings growth. Its valuation also appears attractive relative to its growth prospects and industry peers, indicating solid upside potential.

Most analysts covering AVGO stock are bullish and maintain a "Strong Buy" recommendation.

news.Title: Here's What $10,000 Invested in Broadcom Will Be Worth by 2028
news.Content:
When investors think about AI chipmakers, they may think first of Nvidia or AMD . However, one competitor that most forget about is Broadcom (NASDAQ: AVGO). Why? It's simple: Broadcom only makes computing units for giant customers, not consumers. However, this is a huge opportunity that shouldn't be ignored, because the growth that Broadcom's management team is guiding for is simply incredible.

If you've got $10,000 sitting around (or any other dollar figure, for that matter), I can think of few better places to invest it, because that $10,000 could be worth $20,000 by the end of 2028.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 14x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

What makes Broadcom different?

AMD and Nvidia make graphics processing units (GPUs) , parallel processors that are great at handling a wide range of computationally heavy workloads. GPUs don't have a weakness, but their potential often goes underutilized. Countless GPUs have been stuck running a single type of workload throughout their service life, which leaves some of their incredible capabilities wasted. AI hyperscalers would be better off using a purpose-built computing chip in these applications, which is where Broadcom steps in.

Broadcom partners with its hyperscaler clients to design custom AI computing units powered by proprietary chips that only have the capacities that the client's workloads require. While these units aren't as flexible as GPUs, they provide far better cost performance than a GPU on properly configured workloads. This helps AI hyperscalers maximize their computing potential at lower cost, which is particularly appealing as funds become harder to come by.

Broadcom has several big-name clients, including Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG) (NASDAQ: GOOGL), Meta Platforms , Anthropic, and OpenAI. While all of its clients are ramping up their AI infrastructure spending, none have had a more successful product than Alphabet. Alphabet and Broadcom collaborated to design the Tensor Processing Unit (TPU). This unit has been around for a while, and has gone through several generations. Google Cloud clients can rent access to TPUs on that computing platform. But TPUs are so impressive that Alphabet has begun to expand beyond leasing their compute power in its data centers, and is now starting to sell them directly to external customers like Meta as well.

Story Continues

Orders for custom AI chips across the board are ramping up, and that's the reason why Broadcom could be an excellent investment to make right now.

Broadcom's chip business will grow about 4x in two years

This year, Broadcom expects its AI semiconductor revenue to come in around $57.6 billion. Next year, that figure is expected to rise to $115 billion. To top it off, Broadcom also has visibility to $230 billion in AI semiconductor revenue by 2028, and has secured the supply chain to deliver on this projection. That's about a fourfold increase in two years, which is simply incredible.

But what will that mean for Broadcom's stock?

Broadcom also has non-AI businesses, but these aren't growing nearly as fast. Wall Street analysts estimate $106 billion in revenue this year, indicating about $48 billion in non-AI revenue. If these businesses grow at a 10% clip in 2027 and 2028, that would indicate $58 billion in non-AI revenue. Altogether, that's about $288 billion in revenue by 2028.

AVGO Revenue (TTM) data by YCharts.

In its most recent quarter, Broadcom generated a 44% profit margin, but let's reduce that to 40% to bake some conservatism into the estimate. Revenue of $288 billion and a 40% profit margin indicates $115 billion in profit. If we assign Broadcom a reasonable 30 times earnings, that would result in a $3.45 trillion company.

Currently, Broadcom is a $1.65 trillion company. So, a $10,000 investment now will easily turn into $20,000 by the end of 2028 if the projections above pan out.

news.Title: Wall Street tumbles as worries about AI trade and high oil prices weigh
news.Content:
(In paragraph 13, corrects years to 2026, not 2025)

By Noel Randewich and Purvi Agarwal

Oct 16 (Reuters) - Wall Street tumbled on Friday, with CoreWeave, Broadcom and other AI-related technology stocks under renewed pressure, while a jump in oil prices spooked ‌traders heading into the weekend.

The Nasdaq was on track for a loss of over 4% for the week, hammered by ‌concerns that debt-laden AI infrastructure companies may not turn profits in time to repay debts, particularly with borrowing costs expected to rise.

Nvidia-backed CoreWeave slumped 12%, bringing its loss ​over the past five sessions to about 25%. The data center operator's bonds also sold off sharply this week, pushing yields above 15%.

Broadcom fell 3.6%, and the PHLX chip index sank 2.5%, on track for its eighth straight day of declines.

Investors on Friday were also watching oil prices jump more than 3% due to Middle East supply worries.

"There is some fear in the market," said Rob Haworth, senior investment strategist at U.S. Bank ‌Wealth Management in Seattle. "High oil prices, in particular, tend ⁠to weigh on the price/earnings multiple of stocks, and so I think you have investors looking to be cautious into the weekend rather than take more risk."

Adding to concerns around AI financing, some current Anthropic investors ⁠and prospective investors are weighing a lower valuation for the company in its upcoming IPO, Reuters reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

The S&P 500 was down 1.22% at 7,649.71 points.

The Nasdaq declined 2.19% to 26,128.13 points, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 0.55% at 51,891.77 points.

Six of ​the ​11 S&P 500 sector indexes declined, led lower by communication services, down 2.52%, ​followed by a 2.38% loss in information technology.

The S&P ‌500 was set for its steepest weekly loss since January, and the Nasdaq was heading for its sharpest weekly fall since June.

Third-quarter earnings season shifts into gear next week with reports from Tesla, Meta Platforms and Procter & Gamble. Analysts on average see quarterly earnings surging over 30%, driven by AI-related megacaps, according to LSEG data.

While the S&P 500 remains up about 12% in 2026, most of that gain has come from AI-related tech stocks, and the index's median component has climbed only about 6%, year to date. About 185 S&P 500 stocks have lost ‌ground in 2026.

Hotter-than-expected consumer and producer inflation reports this week showed price pressures ​were extending beyond energy commodities.

Story Continues

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh on Friday voiced optimism ​about US economic strength and surprise about how well global economies ​have been "hanging in there" during a lingering energy shock and tighter monetary policy to fight inflation.

Markets increasingly expect ‌the Fed to keep interest rates unchanged this month. ​Barclays now expects 25-basis-point hikes each ​in December and January.

Tesla dropped 2.5% after the electric-vehicle maker unveiled a redesigned Roadster, powered by rocket-style thrusters, developed in collaboration with SpaceX.

Netflix appointed former Disney executive Peter Rice as chief content officer on Thursday. Its shares were down 2.9%.

Declining stocks outnumbered ​rising ones within the S&P 500 by a ‌1.3-to-one ratio.

The S&P 500 posted 19 new highs and one new low; the Nasdaq recorded 49 new highs and 263 ​new lows.

(Reporting by Tharuniyaa Lakshmi and Purvi Agarwal in Bengaluru, and by Noel Randewich in San Francisco; additional reporting ​by Vidya Ranganathan; Editing by Joyjeet Das, Shinjini Ganguli and David Gregorio)
